title: Written revelation is sacred theology's first principle; it is called Sacred Scripture
english: I. What the prophets and Apostles committed to the sacred letters is written revelation — sacred theology's first principle. From that written deposit the dogmas of the faith and of Christian life are first drawn, and every dispute about revealed things is finally resolved back into it. In that sense we call it Sacred Scripture.

title: Scripture is the analytic, proper, spiritual principle that settles controversy; without analytic ministry no spiritual proof
english: This is an analytic principle — proper (οἰκεῖον), native to the discipline, and spiritual — by which every theological and spiritual controversy is to be decided. For just as from the analytics, or even from the whole philosophy of Aristotle, Plato, and others, though you pound such learning in a mortar, you still cannot draw out and elicit a single spiritual proof to confirm the articles of faith, nor solidly refute the spiritual errors of the Arians, the papal party, and other sectaries — so, on the other side, it is most truly said that without the ministry of analytic doctrine, which admits into theology nothing but what is proper (οἰκεῖον) and native, or what theology itself presupposes in other disciplines as agreeing with spiritual things and analogous to the faith (for this is to analyze, ἀναλύειν, in theology, [[1 Corinthians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:13]]), no controversy's truth can be accurately and solidly proved, taught, or known, nor its falsity struck down and confuted — whether the dispute has been raised in philosophy or in theology.

That analytic gift either falls to excellent natural talents — though only to a few, and imperfectly — or more firmly, from a stronger principle, is granted by the Holy Spirit to some, as to the Apostles, in a more divine mode, or finally is acquired by precepts and teaching; and that teaching is a surer guide than nature. On both sides we are warned to use proper principles for proving the proper theorems of a discipline — philosophical principles for philosophical things, theological for theological. Only so can and should philosophical matters be treated philosophically, and theological matters theologically.

title: Analytic doctrine is handmaid not mistress; ignorance of analytics breeds false spiritual proofs and obstinate heresy
english: So if to the analytic doctrine Aristotle hands down in the Organon we assign not a magisterium but only a ministry and service in seeking the truth of controversies — and if, with Jacopo Zabarella, who holds that the analytic species of logic, when applied to the disciplines, migrates into them, we still concede no metamorphosis of analytics inside theology — no one may fairly object that we are hunting analytic doctrine as mistress of knowing heavenly truth. It is only a handmaid; even when applied to theological matters it remains handmaid of the prince and Lady Theology.

But want of training in the analytics (ἀπαιδευσία τῶν ἀναλυτικῶν) in theology is nothing other than inability to tell apart, on the one hand, what needs proof from what is indemonstrable, and on the other, true proofs from false and pseudographic ones — and likewise theology's own proofs from alien and foreign ones. This is the most fertile mother of ψευδογραφήματα, false spiritual demonstrations, which breed ἄγνοιαν κατὰ διάθεσιν — the ignorance of a vicious affection in heretics and sectaries — altogether contrary to true knowledge or science of spiritual things. Just as that true knowledge is drawn from theology's true and proper principles, so by ignorance of a vicious affection we are seduced when we reason from false and foreign principles. Hence sectaries clutch their errors no less tenaciously, tooth and nail, than the orthodox defend the truth of their judgment, and think they certainly know what in fact they do not know. The same want of analytic training is also mother of many other errors in theology.

title: Mixing philosophical principles into the articles of faith overturns theology; the Word of God is the common rule of faith
english: For when theology's own native proofs are confused with heterogeneous and foreign ones — when philosophical principles and the decrees of human reason are dragged beyond their servant role and twisted to prove spiritual theorems and articles of faith — theology is almost wholly overturned, no less deadly to the human race and to the salvation of souls than any plague, however fierce, is to bodily health. If almost the whole swarm (σμῆνος) of the papal party, whom they commonly call scholastics, had not mixed philosophy with Theology, and had not, through ignorance (ἄγνοιαν) of analysis, transferred the principles philosophy claims by right of property to the proving of spiritual things — and if, leaving philosophical matters aside, they had rightly fitted spiritual things to spiritual theorems — there would have been less to this day of execrable errors and of collisions (συρράξεων) ruinous to the church and to be mourned from the deepest vitals; and God's glory and Christ's most precious merit would have been less obscured, as all the orthodox earnestly complain.

But if this first principle is not settled, whatever is done and disputed is in vain, as Nicephorus Gregoras rightly holds (Roman History, book 10, p. 236). For no dispute can go forward unless we first agree with our adversaries in some common principle. And among us and all heretics whatsoever it is agreed that the Word of God is the rule of faith from which dogmas are to be judged — a common principle conceded by all, from which the arguments are drawn, as Bellarmine says in the preface to Disputation 1. In every theological discourse we teach that the first, proper, native, and unmoved principle on which a mind endowed with a sense of piety should rest today, against the papal party and others, is this: Whatever Sacred Scripture teaches is infallibly true.

title: Against the papal first principle: whatever the Roman pontiff determines is not primary, for they prove it from Scripture
english: Reason 1 compares our principle with the papal party's first claim: Whatever the Roman pontiff determines is infallibly true. Bellarmine and the other Jesuits treat that claim as the only principle. Whatever authority others in the papal Catholic Roman Church still distribute, the Jesuits today gather onto one Pontiff alone.

Yet that claim cannot stand first. They themselves try to prove it from elsewhere — from Sacred Scripture ([[Matthew 16:18 >> Bible:Matthew 16:18]]; [[John 21:15 >> Bible:John 21:15]]-[[John 21:17 >> Bible:John 21:17]]; [[Matthew 10:2 >> Bible:Matthew 10:2]]); they ground tradition on [[John 16:12 >> Bible:John 16:12]], [[1 Corinthians 11:23 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 11:23]], [[2 Thessalonians 2:2 >> Bible:2 Thessalonians 2:2]] and [[2 Thessalonians 2:15 >> Bible:2 Thessalonians 2:15]]; and they ground the Church or bishops in a universal council on [[Matthew 23:2 >> Bible:Matthew 23:2]], [[Matthew 28:20 >> Bible:Matthew 28:20]], and [[Luke 10:16 >> Bible:Luke 10:16]]. Clearer than day, then: their slogans — Whatever the Roman pontiff, traditions, Church, or council hand down is infallibly true — are dragged back to our principle as something prior, though by a false reading, and so cannot be first.

title: Circular reasoning when Scripture's authority hangs on Pope, Church, traditions, and councils
english: 2. From inconvenience or absurdity. Refuse our principle and you either circle or beg the question — the papal party's habit. They hang Scripture's authority on Pontiff, Church, traditions, and councils as far as our knowing goes, and then prove those very authorities from the Scriptures. That is nothing but driving their own proofs around a circle.

They hold Scripture true because Church or Pontiff delivers it; then hold Church or Pontiff true because Scripture says so. Call it what you will: it is not a regress. It is a circle. On that circle's nature see Jacopo Zabarella, book 1, preface to the Analytics, controversy 23.

title: The Bereans; Moses, the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles prove from Scripture
english: 3. Take the Bereans. Day by day, and with praise, they tested against the Scriptures whether Paul's and Silas's preaching held ([[Acts 17:11 >> Bible:Acts 17:11]]). If Paul's doctrine could lawfully — and praiseworthily — be examined by Scripture, how much more may the Pope's determinations be brought to that same test? In the order of our knowing, then, it is plainer that Scripture does not deceive than that the Roman Church or the Pontiff does not.

4. Moses, the Prophets, Christ himself, and the Apostles show the same proving practice, and Scripture itself presses the same warnings. Moses: do whatever the priests teach you according to the Lord's law ([[Deuteronomy 24:8 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 24:8]]). Isaiah: to the law and to the testimony ([[Isaiah 8:20 >> Bible:Isaiah 8:20]]). David in [[Psalm 119 >> Bible:Psalm 119]]: blessed are those who search God's testimonies. Christ answers the resurrection-denying Sadducees from the sacred letters alone ([[Matthew 22:29 >> Bible:Matthew 22:29]]; [[Mark 12:24 >> Bible:Mark 12:24]]), and the Pharisees likewise ([[Matthew 22:43 >> Bible:Matthew 22:43]]-[[Matthew 22:44 >> Bible:Matthew 22:44]]). John the Baptist points to Isaiah as witness of his calling ([[Matthew 3:3 >> Bible:Matthew 3:3]]). Across their epistles the Evangelists and Apostles both allege law and prophets for the articles of faith and proclaim Scripture's authority as a whole ([[2 Peter 1:19 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:19]]; [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:17]]).

These witnesses — and countless more that could be stacked here — seal the analytic proving we press against the papacy and other sophists. The whole method is this: theologians confirm theological and spiritual theorems, and the articles of faith, theologically — from Sacred Scripture's own principles — as the Apostle, teacher of the Gentiles, required in [[1 Corinthians 2:4 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:4]] and [[1 Corinthians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:13]]. No one is more analytic (ἀναλυτικώτερος) than he. First, he names the kind of proof by which he fixed the Corinthians' articles of faith: ἀπόδειξις, a spiritual demonstration that works in the soul. Second, he names what kind of conclusion and principles that demonstration must have: he fits spiritual principles to the spiritual or theological theorems that hold the articles of faith — not λόγοις ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας, the reasons of human wisdom that deceiving philosophy hands over.

title: Analogy with naturally known principles; Scripture's spiritual efficacy; affections and parts to be considered
english: 5. From the analogy of principles known by nature. (1) Principles are such that everyone who knows the terms also knows them to be true. Picture it this way. Admit the light of reason — as child or elder, scholar or unlettered — and you also admit the principles known by the habit philosophers call νοῦν, intellect. Admit the light of divine revelation, and confess under that Author some divinely inspired discipline, and you also admit Sacred Scripture. No Christian, learned or unlearned, denies our principle or puts it in doubt. Doubt Scripture's truth and you forfeit the name of a true Christian — just as the man who denies nature's known principles hardly deserves the name of a sound, reason-using human being.

(2) Those natural principles are not demonstrated and cannot be. They are grasped as true without arguments, from bare consideration of the terms, by their own evidence. So too our theological principle must not — and cannot — be directly demonstrated. The Christian, lit by Christian faith, assents by the Holy Spirit's power, persuaded in the struggle by Scripture itself as he reads it or hears it opened, and with a learner's zeal weighs it attentively according to his spiritual age. Scripture carries an inward force, planted by its Author, that draws and convinces human minds according to each one's age ([[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]]; [[Matthew 7:28 >> Bible:Matthew 7:28]]-[[Matthew 7:29 >> Bible:Matthew 7:29]]; [[John 6:68 >> Bible:John 6:68]]).

What evidence is for principles known by the intellect's habit, that spiritual efficacy is for Christ's words and the sacred Scriptures — an efficacy that shows itself in the struggle of spirit and flesh according to each attentive, pious reader's spiritual measure and age ([[1 Corinthians 2:4 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:4]]-[[1 Corinthians 2:5 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:5]], [[1 Corinthians 2:12 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:12]]-[[1 Corinthians 2:14 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:14]]; [[Ephesians 4:11 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:11]]-[[Ephesians 4:25 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:25]]).
II. Sacred Scripture's affections and parts are to be considered.
